title: Machine-learning myoelectric motor execution partially restores thumb and wrist movement in a paralyzed replanted arm
summary: A 72-year-old with a paralyzed replanted arm regained active thumb and wrist movement after 18 sessions of ML-decoded motor execution.
account: A 72-year-old man's right arm was replanted after a traumatic above-elbow amputation. He had no functional recovery after conventional rehabilitation and developed chronic neuropathic pain. The arm had been replanted at Sahlgrenska University Hospital in Mölndal, Sweden. The Mölndal-based Center for Bionics and Pain Research / Sahlgrenska University Hospital (C.A.R.E.) team then delivered 18 sessions of myoelectric motor execution over 84 days. Nine included sensory training with tactile grids (the paper does not name the treatment site). Eight channels of electromyography were classified by a linear discriminant analysis classifier (Neuromotus, Integrum AB). Intended movements were decoded from the replanted arm and shown on screen as virtual limbs and games. He regained active thumb extension (4 degrees) and active wrist flexion (6 degrees) and extension (10 degrees), movements absent before treatment. Pain fluctuated with no consistent change. Treatment dates are not given, so the publication date (23 November 2024) is used.
purpose: Rehabilitate a highly impaired replanted arm and reduce neuropathic pain using decoded motor intention as feedback
system: Myoelectric motor execution with sensory training: Neuromotus 8-channel EMG and LDA classifier driving virtual limbs and serious games
model_version: Neuromotus (Integrum AB) with linear discriminant analysis classifier
developer: Center for Bionics and Pain Research / University of Gothenburg (academic clinical team); device by Integrum AB
deployer: Center for Bionics and Pain Research and Sahlgrenska University Hospital (C.A.R.E.), Mölndal; treatment site not named in the paper
segment: Patients with replanted or transplanted limbs

ratings.reason: An identifiable patient regained active thumb and wrist movement conventional rehabilitation had not produced. Gains are small and pain did not consistently improve, so no deeper rating is supported.
Single case; authors present it as a potential treatment needing further study.

ai_role.statement: The LDA classifier decodes intended movements from weak EMG in a hand and wrist with no active motion. That is the only way the patient could receive real-time feedback on his motor attempts. The authors attribute the regained movement to this motor execution training. Two authors hold a pending patent on the technology.

evidence.title: Myoelectric pattern recognition with virtual reality and serious gaming improves upper limb function in chronic stroke: a single case experimental design study
evidence.quote: All participants improved upper limb function assessed by FMA-UE (Tau-U 0.72-1.0), and five out of six improved beyond the minimal clinical important difference (MCID).

produced_by: Residual EMG detectable in the impaired limb
Classifier trained on the patient's own signals each session
Repeated sessions with virtual-limb and game feedback
must_hold: Intact or reinnervated muscle producing separable EMG patterns
Clinician-run sessions several times a week
Patient motivation to attempt movements without visible motion

echoes.setting: Six people with chronic stroke, 18 sessions of myoelectric pattern recognition with VR and gaming (single-case experimental design)
echoes.source: Munoz-Novoa et al. (2025) J NeuroEng Rehabil, PMID 39825410

headline: Neuromotus EMG decoding restores thumb and wrist movement
metric: active thumb extension (4 degrees) and active wrist flexion (6 degrees)

comparator.against: the arm's function before treatment, after conventional rehabilitation
comparator.before: no active movement prior the MME interventions
comparator.after: active extension of the thumb (4 degrees) and regained active wrist movement (flex: 6 degrees, extend: 10 degrees)
comparator.quote: regained active extension of the thumb (4 degrees) and regained active wrist movement (flex: 6 degrees, extend: 10 degrees), both of which had no active movement prior the MME interventions

later.note: No follow-up beyond the final session is reported.
